cards.question: The major Campylobacter species causing human cases is {{c1::Campylobacter jejuni}}.

cards.explanation: The percentage in the source is approximate and depends on population and surveillance.

cards.question: A key food vehicle for campylobacteriosis is undercooked {{c1::poultry}}.

cards.explanation: This is a complication of infection rather than direct proof of bacteria residing in nerves.

cards.explanation: Poultry, livestock, birds and reptiles are examples of reservoirs.
cards.text: Salmonella naturally inhabits the {{c1::gastrointestinal tract}} of many animals.
cards.question: Salmonella naturally inhabits the {{c1::gastrointestinal tract}} of many animals.

cards.explanation: The lecture uses this to connect food-chain prevention with infection risk.

cards.explanation: Species identification alone does not determine the disease mechanism.
cards.text: Different disease-associated forms of E. coli are called {{c1::pathotypes}}.
cards.question: Different disease-associated forms of E. coli are called {{c1::pathotypes}}.

cards.explanation: Food does not have to be meat to acquire an animal-associated pathogen.

cards.question: Faecal contamination of irrigation water or manure can transmit E. coli to {{c1::salad produce}}.

cards.question: The non-motile Gram-negative hospital-associated rod described is {{c1::Acinetobacter baumannii}}.

cards.question: An infection acquired in a healthcare setting is {{c1::nosocomial}}.

cards.question: Tuberculosis is caused by {{c1::Mycobacterium tuberculosis}}.

cards.question: A typical primary syphilis chancre is {{c1::painless}}.

cards.question: A rash involving palms and soles suggests {{c1::secondary syphilis}} in the appropriate context.

cards.question: The clinically silent period of syphilis is the {{c1::latent stage}}.

cards.explanation: Treponemal tests such as TPPA are examples; dark-field microscopy requires suitable lesions and is not a latent-stage screening test.

cards.question: Latent syphilis is investigated using {{c1::serological testing}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture highlights cardiovascular and neurological involvement. Neurosyphilis can also occur earlier; stages are not an absolute timetable.

cards.question: Late syphilis can produce severe {{c1::organ damage}} years after infection.

cards.question: Painful chancroid is caused by {{c1::Haemophilus ducreyi}}.

cards.question: Donovanosis is caused by {{c1::Klebsiella granulomatis}}.

cards.question: The characteristic microscopic inclusions in donovanosis are {{c1::Donovan bodies}}.

cards.question: Ureaplasma species lack a {{c1::cell wall}}.

cards.question: The Neisseria species usually associated with meningitis but also capable of urethritis is {{c1::N. meningitidis}}.

cards.question: Absence of gonorrhoea symptoms does not exclude {{c1::infection}}.

cards.question: The genital infection called chlamydia is commonly caused by {{c1::Chlamydia trachomatis}}.

cards.question: Untreated genital chlamydial infection may damage reproductive tissues and contribute to {{c1::infertility}}.

slides.text:
LS5008 / LS5030Examples of Medically ImportantBacterial Infections
Dr Lewis C. E. Mason BSc (Hons), MSc, PhD, MSRB, FIBMS, AFHEA

Learning objectives
Recall specific bacterial infections and theircausative agents

Explain how virulence factors influencesymptomology

Critically evaluate research on medicallyimportant bacterial infections

Starter Activity
What concept do all these images together represent?

WHO Bacterial Priority Pathogens List 2024
WHO (2024) https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240093461

Pseudomonas aeruginosa
A Gram-negative,biofilm-forming, opportunistichealthcare-associated pathogen

Particularly associated with artificial nails, & moist, wet environments

Can cause severe fever, respiratorydistress, and lead to sepsis in individuals - especially newborns

Campylobacter spp.
Gram-negative, comma-shaped, motile, bacterial cause of food borne illness in the UK

Roughly 80% of human casesoriginate from contaminated poultry,especially undercooked chicken

Campylobacter jejuni causes thevast majority of cases (around 88%)

Campylobacter jejuni is also responsible for Guillain-Barré syndrome, a neurological complication of campylobacteriosis infection (see the endotoxins lecture for more info on mechanisms.)

Salmonella spp.
Salmonella spp. are Gram-negative,rod-shaped, motile bacteria

The primary natural reservoir of Salmonella is the GI tract of poultry,cattle, pigs, birds, rodents, and reptiles

‘British Lion Mark’ eggs mean all hens have been vaccinated againstSalmonella, among other requirements

Undercooked, imported eggs are a known sourceof Salmonella spp. outbreaks in the UK

Escherichia coli
Escherichia coli is a Gram-negative, rod-shaped(bacillus) bacterium
There are many different pathotypes of E. coli

Animal droppings on food products (like eggs) cantransmit Escherichia coli

Cows, sheep, goats, deer, and elk carryE. coli naturally in their intestines asymptomatically

E. coli can even appear in salads due to irrigation,nearby animal activity, manure, and food handlers

Acinetobacter baumanii
Gram-negative, rod-shaped, aerobic, non-motilebacterium

Primarily found in healthcare and hospital environments (nosocomial infection)

Thrives on hard surfaces, medical equipment(catheters, ventilators, intravenous lines), and even sinks 

Outbreaks are unfortunately common inintensive care units (ICUs) and wards withimmunocompromised patients

Mycobacterium tuberculosis
The causative agent of tuberculosis (TB), aninfection primarily of the lungs

Has a very waxy cell wall, rich in mycolic acids

Humans are the primary natural reservoirfor the bacteria

TB is one of the leading causes of deathby infectious disease globally

India, Pakistan, Romania, Somalia, and Eritrea are the top countries of origin for non-UK-born TB cases (UKHSA, 2025)

M. tuberculosis in a sputum sample

Treponema pallidum (syphilis)
Treponema pallidum is a species of Gram-negative, spiral-shaped, highly motile bacterium which causes the disease: syphilis

 The disease has up to four stages

 The bacterium is notoriously difficultto culture, and requires co-cultivationwith Sf1Ep rabbit epithelial cells

Syphilis is generally easily treatable with penicillin G

Syphilis – Primary Stage (1)
Usually appears around ten days to three-months after first infection

Usually characterised by a single, small, painless sore or ulcer

Swollen lymph glands may alsoaccompany this

Syphilis – Secondary Stage (2)
A non-itchy rash may appear on thepalms of the hand and/or soles of the feet

Swollen lymph glands may accompany this

Flu-like symptoms may appear

May present with fatigue, fever, patchy hair-loss, lesions, sore throat, and muscle aches 
Hughes (2020) BMJ Case Reports
Whiting (2023) American Journalof Clinical Dermatology

Syphilis – Latent Stage (3)
The latent stage is the ‘hidden’, asymptomatic stage of syphilis following the secondary stage

The latent stage can last for years and even decades

There are no visible signs or symptoms 

Diagnosed through serological testing, confirmed with Fluorescent Treponemal AntibodyAbsorption (FTA-ABS) or Treponema pallidumparticle agglutination assay (TPPA)
Dark-field microscopy rapiddiagnostic test for syphilis

Syphilis – Late Stage (4)
Occurs around 10 – 30 years after first becoming infected with syphilis 

This stage is extremely serious, resulting in severe damage to thebrain, heart, nerves, and otherorgans

The syphilis is usually non-contagious at this stage

Haemophilus ducreyi (chancroid)
Chancroid is caused by Haemophilusducreyi, a Gram-negative, non-motile,rod-shaped species of bacterium

Unlike syphilis, chancroid usuallypresents as multiple, extremely painful sores, and has a shorterincubation period of 1 – 14 days

Haemophilus ducreyi is more commonin lower-income nations, particularlyin sub-Saharan Africa (e.g., Malawi)

Klebsiella granulomatis (donovanosis)
Klebsiella granulomatis is a species ofGram-negative, non-motile, encapsulatedrod-shaped bacterium

May cause significant damage to theskin and deeper tissue layers

Treated with azithromycin or doxycycline

Confirmed by observing ‘Donovan bodies’in tissue samples under the microscope 
Example of Donovan body

Ureaplasma spp. (ureaplasmosis)
Bacteria of the Ureaplasma genus are also able to cause urethritis.They have no cell wall.

They may cause painful urination, unusual discharge, pain in the pelvis, and itching

It can cause infertility in both men and women

Can be carried as part of the normal microbiome, where overgrowth is associated with disease symptoms

Mycoplasma genitalium (Mgen)
Mycoplasma genitalium is another species of bacterium,devoid of a cell wall, capable of causing a range of symptoms (urethritis, proctitis, etc.)

Characterised by unusual discharge, pain during sex, pain in the lower abdomen, bleeding after sexual intercourse, andburning when urinating

Usually treated with doxycycline and azithromycin

Neisseria meningitidis (urethritis & proctitis)




Neisseria meningitidis is a Gram-negative, aerobic, non-motile, bean-shaped, diplococcus-arranged bacterium

While usually associated with meningitis, it is now known to also be an emerging sexually transmissible bacterium

It can cause urethritis and/or proctitis, with a similarpurulent discharge to gonorrhoea, but tends to be far more invasive and can lead to severe complications (e.g., gangrene)

Neisseria gonorrhoeae (gonorrhoea)




Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a Gram-negative speciesof diplococcus-arranged, non-motile, non-spore-forming,bacterium

Gonorrhoea is asymptomatic in around 10% of men and >50% of women

It may cause painful/burning urination, unusual discharge (white/yellow/green) from the penis, vagina, rectum, anus, or throat

The incubation period is usually 2 – 8 days

Chlamydia trachomatis (Chlamydia)
Chlamydia trachomatis is a species of Gram-negative, non-motile, coccus-shaped bacterium

Asymptomatic carriage is possible, with 50% and 80% of infected men and women reporting no symptoms, respectively

The bacterium can cause inflammation of the genital tract,severe reproductive damage, infertility, conjunctivitis, reactive arthritis, urethritis, tonsilitis, swollen lymph glands, etc.

Shigella spp. (shigellosis)
Shigella is a genus of Gram-negative, non-motile, rod-shaped, facultative-anaerobic bacteria. Known to cause the faecal-oral, sexuallytransmissible, bloody diarrhoeal disease: shigellosis (dysentery)

There are four species in the Shigella genus:- Shigella sonnei- Shigella flexneri- Shigella boydii- Shigella dysenteriae

Its inoculum dose is extraordinarily low (10 – 100 CFU)
Within each species, there may be more than oneserotype (e.g., Shigella flexneri 3a), defined by theO-antigen repeat region of the cell wall lipopolysaccharide (LPS)




Shigella sonnei Gram-stain

Shigella spp. symptoms
Species of the Shigella genus cause shigellosis, a severegastrointestinal illness characterised by bloody, potentiallymucus-filled, foul-smelling diarrhoea

Frequent passing of small volumes of diarrhoea is also common in shigellosis

A painful feeling of needing to empty the bowels, even when there is nothing left to excrete (tenesmus) is highly indicative of shigellosis

The incubation period can be as little as 24 hourspost-inoculation

Shigella spp. diagnosis
As shigellosis presents as bloody diarrhoea, patients mayattend Accident & Emergency (A&E) in a hospitalrather than a sexual health clinic

Culturing of stool for Shigella spp. is the gold standard for shigellosis diagnosis
Molecular testing (PCR) is more rapid by identifying the ipaH gene, but caution is needed here as some E. coli may also carry this gene…

A major aid in diagnosing a patient with shigellosis is the context,which is why it is important to ask the patient about their recent travel history and sexual activity history

Mason et al., 2026Microbial Genomics
Geographical distribution of sexually transmitted shigellosis
Think critically – do you really think this is a true / ‘real’ distribution?

Plenary Activity
Suggest all the potential sources of bacterial infection associated with this image

Name somebacterial generaand species too

Summary
There are many medically importantbacterial species; we have just focused on a small subset of them

Even members of the same speciescan cause completely different disease symptomologies

One Health is an increasingly recognised concept warranting furtherinvestigation and research
